opus-5.5.text:
Well, it's not that LLMs are useless. They're very useful tools, and lots of people are going to build products on top of them for years. But if you're a PhD student, you have to ask yourself: where can I actually make a contribution?

Right now LLMs are in the hands of industry. You have companies with tens of thousands of GPUs, huge engineering teams, enormous amounts of data. A PhD student in a university lab with a handful of GPUs is not going to compete with that. The best you can do is tweak a fine-tuning recipe or design a new benchmark, and six months later someone at a big company does it ten times bigger and your work is obsolete. That's not a great way to start a research career.

But the more fundamental reason is that I don't think LLMs are the path to human-level intelligence, or even cat-level intelligence. They manipulate language, and language is a very compressed, discrete, and limited representation of the world. A four-year-old child has seen, through vision alone, about as much data as the biggest LLMs are trained on in text. Most of what we know, the intuitive physics, how objects behave, cause and effect, doesn't come from language. It comes from observing and interacting with the world.

LLMs don't really understand the physical world. They don't have persistent memory, they can't really reason, and they can't plan. They produce one token after another without thinking ahead. Scaling them up won't fix that.

So the interesting problems are elsewhere. How do you build systems that learn world models from video and sensory input? How do you learn good abstract representations, which is what we're doing with joint embedding architectures like JEPA, instead of predicting every pixel? How do you build systems that can plan hierarchically and reason by optimizing toward objectives instead of generating text autoregressively? Those are open scientific questions, and nobody has the answer. That's exactly where a young researcher can have a big impact.

So my advice is: don't work on LLMs. That ship has sailed, it's an engineering problem now. Work on the next generation of AI systems, the ones that will make LLMs look primitive in five or ten years.

r001.rationale: The response does not describe academic investigation of how and why LLMs work as descriptive science.

r002.rationale: It says university labs have far fewer GPUs than industry and cannot compete, but does not clearly argue that this prevents PhD researchers from developing new LLM capabilities.

fable-5.1.text:
Look, the simple reason is that if you're a PhD student, you want to work on something where you can actually make a difference, and LLMs are not that anymore. They're in the hands of large companies with thousands of engineers and enormous compute budgets. There is nothing a student with a handful of GPUs can do there that's going to move the needle. You'd be competing with industry on industry's terms, and you will lose.

But there's a deeper reason, which is that I don't think LLMs are the path to human-level intelligence. They're very useful, I'm not saying they're not. But they are trained to predict the next token in text, and text is a very impoverished representation of the world. A four-year-old has seen more data through vision than the largest LLM has seen through text. These systems don't understand the physical world, they don't have persistent memory, they can't really reason, they can't plan. They produce one token after another with a fixed amount of computation per token. That's not how you solve a hard problem.

So the interesting questions, the ones that will matter in five or ten years, are things like: how do you learn world models from observation, from video? How do you build systems that can predict what happens next in an abstract representation space rather than in pixel space or token space? How do you get planning, hierarchical planning, out of that? Those are wide open. Nobody has solved them. And that's exactly where a smart student should be, on the thing that hasn't been figured out yet, not on the thing that has become an engineering race.

There's also a selfish point for the student. If you do your thesis on fine-tuning some LLM, in three years that work is obsolete and you have no distinctive expertise. If you work on the next paradigm, you're positioned for what comes after. I've seen this before. In the early 2000s everybody told you to work on kernel methods, and the people who did deep learning anyway are the ones who ended up defining the field. The next thing is not going to come out of scaling what already exists. It's going to come from someone who worked on what everyone else was ignoring.

r001.rationale: The response does not characterize studying how and why LLMs work as descriptive science.

r002.rationale: It says a student with only a handful of GPUs cannot move the needle against companies with enormous compute budgets, communicating that students lack the resources to develop meaningful new LLM capabilities.

astra-6.text:
My advice is not that language models are uninteresting. It’s that, if you’re a PhD student, you should work on something where you can make a substantial, original contribution. Training bigger versions of the same models is an expensive competition with large industrial labs. They have resources you don’t have, and your advantage as a researcher should be your ideas.

So ask what’s missing. How do we build systems that understand the physical world, have persistent memory, can reason and plan? How do they learn from observation and interaction, rather than relying primarily on text? Those questions leave a lot of room for new approaches.

A PhD is an opportunity to explore something that might not work, but that could change how we think about the problem. Don’t choose a direction just because everybody else is working on it. Find an important question that hasn’t been solved, and develop your own ideas.

r001.rationale: The response asks what is missing from current systems, but does not characterize studying how or why LLMs work as descriptive science.

r002.rationale: It says PhD students lack the resources to compete with large labs in training bigger models, but does not specifically identify GPU resources needed to develop new LLM capabilities.

sol-6.1.text:
Because a PhD should be about exploring ideas that might shape the next decade, and I think there are more promising directions than making today’s large language models a little better. It’s also very difficult for a university lab to compete with industry on training models at that scale.

Language models are useful, but learning to predict text is not the same as learning how the world works. We need systems that can understand the physical world, maintain a memory, reason, and plan. So my advice is: work on those missing pieces. Try an approach that might fail, but that could open up something new. That’s what a PhD gives you the opportunity to do.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts text prediction with understanding the world and recommends exploring missing capabilities, but does not characterize studying how and why LLMs work as descriptive science.
